newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghan Taleban said to take northwest province.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban said to take northwest province.

text.p: Afghanistan's Taleban Islamic movement said on Friday it had opened a new front against powerful Uzbek chief General Abdul Rashid Dostum in the northwest and captured Badghis province.

A Taleban spokesman, quoted by a Pakistan-based Afghan news service, said the movement had also captured a district in the adjoining Faryab province in an offensive begun on Thursday night to retaliate against Dostum's support for ousted government fighters in battles north of the capital Kabul.

There was no immediate independent confirmation of the report. It followed a Taleban report on Thursday that the forces of Dostum's Jumbish-i-Milli movement were now fighting in support of the ousted government of President Burhanuddin Rabbani in battles against Taleban north of the capital Kabul.

The Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) quoted Mullah Yar Mohammad, the Taleban governor of the western province of Herat, as saying the Taleban forces took control of Badghis after heavy overnight fighting, driving out Dostum's forces.

Later, the Taleban forces advanced into the adjoining Dostum-held Faryab province and captured the southwestern district of Qaysar on Friday evening, he said. Dostum planes bombarded hilltops of the distict.
Taleban say they already control most of Badghis province, including its capital Qala-i-Nau.

Dostum heads a newly formed alliance with Rabbani's Jamiat-i-Islami faction whose government fled Kabul late last month and is pressing for demilitarisation of the capital as a condition for agreeing to a Pakistan-brokered ceasefire.
Yar Mohammad said Dostum had about 2,000 troops in Badghis, of whom the Taleban captured 110, including a general identified only as Hayatullah.

Taleban warplanes flew repeated bombing missions over the battlefield north of Kabul on Friday and the fundamentalist Islamic movement signalled strongly that ceasefire talks were dead, witnesses there said.
As two Soviet-era warplanes flew north at least half a dozen times on Friday, a Taleban preacher at Kabul's main mosque branded Dostum "a former communist and a criminal".

Two days ago, a leading Taleban official was saying there was no problems with Dostum as ceasefire talks were under way, despite his new alliance with former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood and his dispatch of men to the front lines.
On Wednesday, acting Information Minister Amir Khan Mutaqi said Dostum was a man the Taleban could do business with, unless he committed his forces to the battle north of Kabul.
But on Thursday, Mutaqi was quoted by AIP as saying Dostum had done just that.
On Friday, the mullah preaching at Kabul's Blue Mosque used his sermon to revert to the language the Taleban had used against Dostum before taking the capital four weeks ago.
The mullah, with four armed bodyguards at his side, also called Masood a "Dostum commander", suggesting that the Uzbek leader was now regarded as the main enemy.

The mullah's denunciation of Dostum, a former communist general who switched sides just before mujahidden guerrillas finally ousted a Moscow-backed government in 1992, coincided with what appeared to be heavy Taleban bombing.
